newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Bradford attacks NZ power distributors.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Bradford attacks NZ power distributors.

text.p: Energy Minister Max Bradford warned power distribution companies on Wednesday against anti-competitive behavior.

"If there are signs that they are doing that, that they are sitting behind local monopolies or near monopolies, then the Commerce Act is there to do it, then I will have no compunction as minister in removing those barriers," Bradford told Reuters.
He was commenting on plans to split up state-owned power generator Electricity Corporation of New Zealand and ensure pricing benefits were passed on to consumers and not taken by distributors.
The government was determined to ensure that the retail power companies were not going to block competition in the electricity market, Bradford said.
He attacked the plan of Auckland power distributor Mercury Energy to takeover, in conjuction with Utilicorp New Zealand, rival Auckland power company Power New Zealand Ltd.
Bradford also queried how the anti-monopolies Commerce Commission allowed the takeover, particularly in view of Utilicorp's control of Waikato's WEL Energy Ltd and Bay of Plenty Electricity.
"I found that a very strange decision given the fact that there are the interlocking ownership issues with Power NZ and these other companies. I just found it extraordinary frankly.

"If you look at Mercury, they are just setting themselves up as a huge monopoly, at least in the lines business, with their relationship with Power New Zealand who in turn have a controlling interest in Bay of Plenty Electricity and WEL Energy," Bradford said.
"My understanding is that Mercury intend to replace all the Power New Zealand directors on those boards and take effective control.
"That from my perspective would be a most regrettable direction in a situation where we are looking for more, not less, competition," he said.
Reuters contacted Mercury for comment but executives were not immediately available.

Bradford said he would consider removing the ban on state-owned power generators entering the retail market and competing directly, although that would not happen while Electricity Corp of New Zealand had its current dominance in generation.

"If the state-owned generators became smaller players in the marketplace then there is an issue of whether they should be put on the same footing as everybody else so that we don't simply shift the monopoly components of the system from the state-owned generation end of the market to privately and community-owned retail power companies," Bradford said.

He said the most likely barrier to competition was the sort of behaviour of some power companies but the real test was whether they were prepared to allow other competitors into their markets in an open way.
"If they can grow by acquisition as some of them have done, then that is much more controlling your own marketplace than truly competing," he said.
"The government is determined to ensure that the retail power companies aren't in a position to block the development of proper competition," he added.
